Madam Chair, distinguished members of the committee, honored guests, my name is Dorothy Gould, but most people call me Dot. I am a member of the Legislative Assembly of the Falkland Islands. Representing the rural community. I hold the Health and Social Services portfolio. I moved to the— with my parents to the Falkland Islands from Devon, England, when I was just 5 years old. They came to work, fell in love with the Falklands, and decided to stay. 3 years later, Argentina invaded our new home. We, as Falkland Islanders, remained throughout the invasion because it is our home, regardless of how long we've been there. From 10 generations to newcomers, that remains the case today. In the community of around 3,600 people, there are people from over 70 countries of birth, from the UK, Zimbabwe, Chile, Argentina, South Africa, the Philippines, Guyana, and more. The Falklands is home to all. We are multicultural, not through implantation, but through a culture built on willingness to welcome others and an adaptable spirit. Every resident of the Falkland Islands, by birth or by choice, receives free healthcare. We fund it ourselves from our own economy. We fund university education for every qualifying student wherever in the world they choose to study. Around 80% of our students return home, almost unheard of for a small island community. Our economy carries an A+ credit rating from S&P Global. We do not ask the United Kingdom for any money. I was 7 years old during the Argentine occupation. I'm not going to rehash 1982, but I want this committee to understand what it feels like as a child to have someone take your home from you. I think of my own children who grew up in the Falkland Islands, and I think about what I want for them: the right to decide their own future and for their representatives to speak in conversations about the future of their home. The United Nations has been considering the question of the Falkland Islands since 1965. In all that time, this committee has never sent a visiting commission to the islands. Not once. Other non-self-governing territories have received visits. We have not, despite extending this invitation repeatedly.
¡Gracias!

We welcome scientists from all over the world to study our environment and wildlife. We welcome tourists, including Argentinians, who I have seen arrive expecting a military outpost and leave having met a peaceful community that just wants to live their lives and determine their own future. A community made up of people like me, my husband, my children, my colleague Michael, whose family have lived on the Falkland Islands for 7 generations, and many others. Falkland Islands children grow up with the land in their hearts. They know to lean against the wind, how to identify the local wildlife, which plants are edible, and how to walk the uneven and rocky ground with quick and confident steps. They aren't taught these things consciously. They absorb them from their parents and grandparents, the way all people who love their home do. Please come to our islands. You will find nearly 1 million penguins, the world's first designated key biodiversity area for sei whales, and species found almost nowhere else on Earth. You will find a community with its own identity, making life work in a remote corner of the world. All we ask is that you see us for ourselves. Thank you.
I thank Miss Dorothy Dot Gould. I now give the floor to Mr. Michael Goss. Sir, you have the floor, please.

Madam Chair, distinguished members of the committee, my name is Michael Goss. I am a 6th generation Falkland Islander, a farmer, mechanical engineer, and a former wildlife guide. Dot has described our community, and I want to talk about this resolution to the committee as it will be considered. This committee is asked year after year to support negotiations between the United Kingdom and Argentina over the future of the Falkland Islands without the inclusion of our people, who Argentina does not recognize. Well, here I am today in front of you alongside Dot. We do exist. We are a reality that has existed for generations. Argentina's own constitution establishes the recovery of sovereignty over the Falkland Islands as a permanent and non-renounceable objective. Their only permitted outcome from any negotiation is the attainment of sovereignty over the islands. That is not a negotiation. That is a transfer of ownership dressed as diplomacy. The Declaration on Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples is clear: All peoples have the right to determine their own political status. Our people have done exactly this. In 2013, we held a referendum. 92% turnout. 99.8% voted to remain a self-governing British Overseas Territory. Argentina's section of the working paper claims no organization observed this referendum. That is incorrect. The referendum was independently observed by an international mission led by the United States, with observers from Canada, Uruguay, Chile, and New Zealand. Their conclusion was unambiguous: the referendum was free and fair. I hold the natural resources portfolio, including our sustainably managed fisheries, which is approximately 58% of our GDP. Beyond our waters lies the Blue Hole, international waters with no regional fisheries management organization no catch limits, and no environmental or workforce protections. This gap exists because Argentina refuses to cooperate, indeed harming their own interests through a refusal to work together. In September of 2024, a cooperation package was agreed between the UK and Argentina covering fisheries data exchange, flight connectivity, and humanitarian cooperation, including a next of kin visit to the Argentine cemetery and continued ICRC work to identify the unidentified remains of Argentine soldiers. The Falkland Islands delivered. In December 2024, Argentine families came to visit their loved ones. We welcomed them. Regrettably, Argentina has not delivered on any of the other agreed terms. The flight has not resumed. Fisheries data exchange has not taken place. We remain willing. I join Dot informally and officially extending an invitation from the Falkland Islands Legislative Assembly to the Decolonisation Committee. Send a visiting mission to the Falkland Islands. Come and see for yourselves. The resolution before this committee uses the word interests. We are asking you to recognize our wishes. Those are not the same word. Interests can be assigned to us by governments that do not speak for us. Wishes must be expressed by us. The difference is between being heard and being spoken for. Article 1 of both UN Covenants on Human Rights, to which both the United Kingdom and Argentina are party, guarantees the right of all peoples to self-determination. We ask only that this principle be applied consistently. We are not asking any delegation to take a position on sovereignty. We only ask that the people of the Falkland Islands have the right to be heard on matters relating to our own future. My family has been in the Falkland Islands since 1841. Dot's family moved to the Islands in 1979 and chose to stay. Between us, we represent what it means to be a Falkland Islander. Born to it or choosing it, we are here. We are real. In closing, I leave you with these words: Our Islands. Our Wishes. Our Right. Our determination. Thank you.

I thank Mr. Goss. Also, in accordance with request for hearing granted by the Special Committee, I now invite Ms. Paula Maria Vernet and Mr. Guillermo Raimundo Clifton to take the seats at the petitioner's table. I now give the floor to Ms. Paula Maria Vernet. Madame, you have the floor, please.

Thank you, Madam President.

Señora Presidente, Madam Chair, distinguished delegates. My name is Paula Vernet, and I am appearing once again before this distinguished committee as an Argentine citizen and as a direct descendant of Luis Vernet, who in 1829 was appointed as the first military and political commander of the Malvinas Islands by the governor of the United Provinces of Río de la Plata. My presence here is not just an individual action. It is the continuation of a story, my family story on the islands. My great-great-great-grandfather Luis Fenley and María Sainz settled on the islands, and they did not come to the islands with a transitory presence. They traveled there to stay. They went with their children and they took with them the objects of an entire life, their furniture, their piano, their household plants. They attempted to build a home in difficult conditions. Vernet worked hard and made many efforts with the aim of developing a community, developed economic activities, and exercised the authority entrusted to him by the Argentine authorities. He did so with the expectation of being able to stay stay, being able to build a future, and being able to grow future generations there as well. That story was abruptly interrupted in 1833 when the Argentine population was forcibly removed. Since then, Argentina's claim has been constant for the state and for the families who, like mine, saw their, their life plans interrupted. My father addressed this committee on numerous occasions, and I am now the one who is taking the floor. And if this dispute is not resolved, my children will come here too, because the Malvinas question is not a question of the past. It is a cause that is passed down intact over time from one generation to the next. We will continue to insist because the Argentine people is a people that chooses to believe, to believe that the passage of time cannot legitimize a situation that originated in an act of force that Argentina protested from the very beginning, believing in diplomatic efforts as well and international law, believing in the justice of our claims, and belief in this committee and the decolonization process. Last year, marked 60 years since the adoption of Resolution 2065, in which this committee recognized that we are facing a sovereignty dispute between Argentina and the United Kingdom, which can be solved through bilateral negotiations, taking into account the interests of the inhabitants of the islands, because the inhabitants of the islands do not constitute a people with a right to self-determination. However, 6 decades on, the United Kingdom continues to refuse to resume that dialogue. As long as the dispute remains pending, we are particularly concerned by recent unilateral licenses for the exploration and potential exploitation of hydrocarbons in the disputed area. The exploitation of our natural resources is nothing new. For years, unilaterally our fisheries resources were taken from us. But this is even more serious because it is a question of non-renewable resources. Given a territorial dispute, the parties should refrain from carrying out actions that could exacerbate or expand it or which could modify the status quo as long as it is awaiting a solution. This is not just a question— an economic question. It is a question of preserving the integrity of a pending decolonization process and avoiding the consolidation of extractive activities, preventing that from generating obstacles that would hinder a just and lasting solution. The natural resources of a territory that is disputed should not be exploited for the exclusive benefit of one of the parties. Cooperation and dialogue are the paths that are promoted by the United Nations. The consolidated of claimed rights is not such a path. Therefore, I respectfully call upon this committee to continue to urge the parties to resume negotiations on the question of sovereignty in accordance with the relevant resolutions of the General Assembly. And I choose to believe that with the necessary political will, this dispute can at long last be resolved and that future generations will not have to come back to this committee to claim what under law continues to be an integral part of Argentine territory.

The—

and this is all to say that the Malvinas, which are an integral part of the Argentine territory, are is closely present within Argentine science because the Malvinas cause is a part of our Argentine identity. In 1833, the United Kingdom occupied by force our Malvinas Islands. They expelled the Argentine— Argentinians in Puerto Luis, and they introduced civilian and military personnel of British origin. From that time until now, the United Kingdom has maintained a strict colonial policy in order to keep the territory under the illegal British administration. The inhabitants of the islands are descendants or members of the colonisation that has been carried out by the United Kingdom. Is not a population that suffered through colonialism. Rather, it is a predominantly British population that benefited, benefited therefrom. The United Nations has never admitted that what applies to the Malvinas question is a principle of self-determination because there is no colonized people there, rather a handful of British citizens on Argentine territory. Madam Chair, it is my wish to ensure that the laudable efforts for— of this committee to bring an end to colonialism in all of its forms reach the Argentine Republic and lead the Argentine Republic and the UK to resume negotiations on the sovereignty dispute into the Malvinas, South Georgia, and South Sandwich Islands and the surrounding maritime areas. This is my profound wish and that of all Argentinians. Thank you very much, Madam Chair.

I thank Mr. Clifton. The special committee has now heard the last petitioner on this item. I now give the floor to the distinguished Permanent Representative of Chile to introduce draft resolution L.8. Excellency, you have the floor.

Please allow me to congratulate you firstly for your reelection and your praiseworthy leadership and stewardship of the work of this Decolonization Committee. We also extend our thanks and our greetings to all members and to the C24 Secretariat for its dedicated work and commitment to the efforts made by this committee. I'd also like to particularly greet here, His Excellency the Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Trade and Worship of the Republic of Argentina, Mr. Pablo Kirchner, and the delegation traveling with him. Madam Chair, on behalf of the delegations of Bolivia, Cuba, Nicaragua, and Venezuela, as well as that of my own delegation, Chile, it is my honor to put before this committee for their consideration the draft resolution on the question of the Malvinas which reflects the main principles of the doctrine that the United Nations has confirmed over the years relating to this special and particular situation in which this Committee has played a pivotal role. This is a draft that reflects the same concepts that more than 60 years ago the United Nations established for the first time as a means to peacefully resolve the sovereignty dispute relating to the Malvinas, South Georgia, and South Sandwich Islands and the surrounding maritime areas. This method is direct dialogue between the sole two parties, that is, the Republic of Argentina and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. Madam Chair, the co-sponsoring countries highlight the validity of the Secretary-General's good offices mission that was entrusted by the General Assembly in 1982, reaffirmed year after year by the Special Committee, to assist both parties with resuming negotiations in order to find a peaceful and lasting solution to the sovereignty dispute relating to the Malvinas, South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands and the surrounding maritime areas. And they urge the Secretariat to inform members of the Committee relating to the development such negotiations through relevant documentation, particularly the working paper on this area. The lasting solution to the question of the Malvinas is a matter of fundamental importance and sensitivity for the nations of Latin America and the Caribbean. This has been made plain in the various fora that bring together our countries, which have adopted joint communiqués and declarations which recall and reiterate our support for the legitimate Argentine rights in the sovereignty dispute relating to this issue. The question of the Malvinas remains present within the regional multilateral agenda. This has been reflected in the statement of the Ibero-American Summit in the Dominican Republic that was held in Santo Domingo on the 25th of March, 2020. And it was also reflected in the special declaration on the question of the Malvinas that was held in November 2023 during the first South American meeting among ministers of defense and foreign affairs, and most recently in the general statement of heads of states and the special declaration on the question of the Malvinas at the 8th CELAC summit that was held in Kingstown, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines on the 1st of March, 2024, which supported the rights of the Argentine Republic in the sovereignty disputes over the Malvinas, South Georgia, South Sandwich Islands, and surrounding maritime areas. In this regard, we reiterate our call on the parties to comply with the General Assembly's mandate to not involve actors outside the sovereignty dispute maintain— keeping this zone of peace and cooperation. All of this within the framework of United Nations resolutions and the provisions and purposes of the UN Charter, including the principle of territorial integrity. Madam Chair, the text that has been presented firstly recognizes that the question of the Malvinas is a, quote, special and particular colonial question which stands out from other colonial situations under the consideration of this Committee due to the existence of a sovereignty dispute between two states, that is, the Republic of Argentina and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. Secondly, the draft resolution recognizes and determines that the only way to bring an end to this special and particular situation is through a negotiated settlement to the dispute between the governments of both countries and requests that the parties enhance their dialogue and cooperation process through the resumption of negotiations. Madam Chair, in this room we have often heard a reiterated statement that the persistence of colonial situations in the midst of the 21st century is an anachronism, anachronism that must be resolved. The question of the Malvinas is one of the representations of colonialism that we continue to see, with regard to which the international community has for more than half a century now been calling for a definitive settlement. My country and the other co-sponsors support the legitimate rights, sovereignty rights of the Republic of Argentina relating to this issue, and we believe that the only way to resolve the dispute is through bilateral negotiations between Argentina and the United Kingdom. To that end, we reiterate the call on the parties in dispute to resume these negotiations as soon as possible, bearing in mind All of the aforementioned—Chile and the other co-sponsoring countries—trust that this Committee, just as it has in other previous years, will adopt the draft resolution by consensus. And further, we are grateful for the trust placed in our delegation for this presentation. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished Permanent Representative of Chile. I now give the floor to His Excellency Pablo Quino, Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Trade, and Worship of Argentina, to address the committee. Excellency, we welcome you and you have the floor, please.

Madam Chair, distinguished members of the committee, observer delegations, ladies and gentlemen. At the outset, Argentina would like to express its condolences and its solidarity to the Venezuelan people in light of the tragedy that occurred yesterday with the two earthquakes. President Milei expressed Argentina's readiness to provide support to Venezuela in these difficult times. Madam Chair, it is an honor to, for the first time, address as Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Argentina, the Special Committee on Decolonization of the United Nations. I bring to this committee the voice of the Republic of Argentina and a people that continues with its irrevocable commitment. The Republic of Argentina maintains with full historic and legal belief its sovereignty over the Malvinas, South Georgia, South Sandwich Islands, and surrounding maritime areas, which were territories that were illegally occupied by the United Kingdom and of Great Britain and Northern Ireland in in 1833. This affirmation expresses a state policy and a national belief that transcends generations. The Malvinas belongs to the deep-rooted history of Argentina, to the integrity of our territory, and to the longstanding mandate of our national constitution. Madam Chair, in 1833, the United Kingdom occupied the islands through an act of force that was never consented to by my country. It, uh, broke with Argentine territorial integrity, expelled the authorities and the legitimately established population. It then proceeded to populate the territory with its own settlers and prevented the settlement of Argentine citizens. This led to a colonial situation that remains to date. Argentina never allowed consent for this occupation and maintains constant peaceful and legal protest. 60 years ago, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 2065. This recognized the existence of a sovereignty dispute between Argentina and the United Kingdom and established that the way to bring an end to this colonial situation is through bilateral negotiations, bearing in mind the interests of the population on the islands. This resolution was a landmark. The international community recognized that the Malvinas question could not be buried under the passage of time and that the dispute demanded a peaceful solution based on dialogue and international law. Pursuant to this mandate, Argentina and the United Kingdom negotiated for 16 years. There were meetings, proposals, and diplomatic dialogue. All of this demonstrated that the path highlighted by the United Nations, what is possible when there is a seriousness, political, uh, decisiveness, and good faith. The appeal to resume negotiations has enjoyed sustained support in different regional and multilateral fora. We have seen this in the Organization of American States, the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States, the Mercosur States Parties and Associated States, the Ibero-American Summit, the Zone of Peace and Cooperation of the South Atlantic, the Brasilia Consensus and the Group of 77 and China, among others. Chair, the United Kingdom repeatedly invokes the principle of self-determination of peoples to evade dialogue. Argentina would like to be clear before this committee: this principle, which is so essential in decolonization processes, does not apply to the Malvinas question. The General Assembly recognized the right to self-determination when it understood that this principle did correspond to the item under review. In the Malvinas question, none of these resolutions referred to the desires of the inhabitants nor to the principle of self-determination. Indeed, in 1985, the General Assembly rejected by overwhelming majority two British attempts to incorporate this principle in the relevant resolution. Self-determination requires the existence of a people subject to colonial domination with the— with a distinct ethnic and cultural identity from that of the occupying power. This pursuant to Resolution 1541 of the General Assembly. On the Malvinas Islands, there is no colonized people. There is a British population implanted by the occupying power following the expulsion by the authorities, um, of the legitimate Argentine inhabitants. The total population of the islands is approximately 3,000 inhabitants. And half of which were born there. At the same time, there are around 1,200 British soldiers stationed there. This reveals the strategic militarized nature of the occupation. Recognizing that the inhabitants of the islands whom the United Kingdom deems to be full British citizens have the power to decide as to the legal condition of the territory that they occupy would mean a misinterpretation of the principle of self-determination. It would also be contrary to Resolution 1514 and international law and decolonization. Along these lines, the referendum convened by the British government in 2013 lacks validity under this organization. It was held without the intervention of the General Assembly, and no state nor international body sent official electoral observers. It did not change the nature of the dispute, nor did it modify any pending obligations. The Argentine position has not seen— does not recognize any indifference with regard to the inhabitants of the islands. The national constitution enshrines respect for their interests and their way of living. Argentina continues with this mandate seriously, responsibly, and with a permanent commitment to peaceful settlement— the peaceful and just settlement of this dispute. Chair, the persistence of this dispute prevents the relationship between Argentina and the United Kingdom growing as deeply as it could. The Argentina aspires to building a mature relationship on this shared history. This relationship demands a particular attention, and it is all the more urgent to talk about the, uh, the acts under the— contrary to Resolution 3149 of the General Assembly, United Kingdom maintains a disproportionate military presence on the— in the South Atlantic, with approximately 1,200 troops stationed on the islands. This is a force equivalent to around 40% of the population of the territory. This reveals the scale of the militarization. The United Kingdom also unilaterally, legally, and illegitimately grants licenses for the exploration and exploitation of natural resources that are both renewable and non-renewable, including hydrocarbon— hydrocarbons and fishing resources in the area under dispute. Argentina has denounced these acts and will continue to do so with all legitimate means. The most worrisome episode was related to the potential beginning of activities in hydrocarbon exploitations in the area under dispute. In December 2025, the illegitimate licensees Rockhopper Exploration PLC and Navitas Petroleum Development and Production Limited made announcements relating to the development of the Sea Lion area that is located in the Malvinas North Pool that is just off the Malvinas Islands. In light of these announcements, the President of Argentina, Javier Milei, instructed me to express my strong rejection of the Argentinian— the Republic of Argentina. Pursuant to this, I reiterate before this committee the Argentine determination to, in accordance with international law, take all necessary measures to safeguard our rights and interests, our own rights and interests. The resources of the South Atlantic are also part of the permanent heritage of the Argentine Republic. They are also part of the responsibilities that our country exercises in one of the most strategic regions in the Southern Hemisphere. No unilateral decision can change an illegitimate occupation nor displace the mandate of the United Nations, Chair. The Republic of Argentina reiterates its full readiness to resume bilateral substantive negotiations with the UK in accordance with Resolution 2065. Our country reaffirms its commitment to the peaceful settlement of disputes with effective multilateralism and with a rules-based international order. For this reason, we call on the United Kingdom to take the— show the same commitment and to comply with the obligations reflected in the relevant resolutions of the General Assembly and this committee. The international— the Malvinas question is a matter for the consciousness of the entire international community. Almost two centuries after an act of force against a young nation during times of peace, the occupying power purports to legitimately— to legally legitimize a situation that began with an illegal occupation. The arguments put forward by the UK to attempt to justify this occupation have changed over the years. The fact that, uh, that this, this, that what gave rise to this dispute has remained unchanged. International law cannot accept that time changes an usurpation through sovereignty. Argentina comes to this committee sure that our demand is, relies on history, law, and justice. We also come for you with the strength of a nation that respects peace and trusts diplomacy as a tool for meetings of peoples. Chair, I'd like to express our special thanks to the Republic of Chile for presenting this resolution. This is a gesture which honors the traditional support in the peace in— of the Malvinas question and reaffirms the importance of the South Atlantic as a zone of peace and cooperation. I also would like to thank those countries that have co-sponsored this resolution and the members of this committee for their sustained work. Every statement of this body keeps alive the essential responsibility of the United Nations to bring an end— bringing an end to colonialism demands constancy, consistency, and upholding law. As a Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Argentina, I am proud to represent the voice of a country which aspires to recover full sovereignty over all of its territory. The Malvinas transcends generation— transcends governments. It is a national cause, a state policy, and a commitment that unites entire generations of Argentinians. Argentina will continue along this path firmly and with an unwavering determination to reach a peaceful, lasting solution to this dispute. It will do this because peace demands law. It will do this because justice demands perseverance. It will do this because the Malvinas forever beat within the heart of our nation through history, through law, and through our belief The Malvinas are Argentine. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Iraq speaking on behalf of G77 and China. I now recognize and give the floor to the distinguished representative of Antigua and Barbuda. Antigua and Barbuda, you have the floor, please.

Madam Chair, Antigua and Barbuda is pleased to participate once again in the work of this special committee. We reaffirm our steadfast commitment to the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations and the continued advancement of the decolonization agenda, which remains central to the organization's enduring responsibility to uphold justice, self-determination, and the peaceful settlement of disputes. On the question of the Falkland Islands, Malvinas, Antigua and Barbuda reiterates its longstanding position as a friend of both Argentina Republic and the United Kingdom. Guided by that friendship, we once again encourage both parties to resume substantive and constructive negotiations aimed at achieving a peaceful resolution of the sovereignty disputes in accordance with the relevant resolution of the United Nations, particularly General Assembly Resolution 2065/20. And the decisions of this Committee.
